paras: The attempted lynching of Eugene Smith took place in Liberty, Sullivan County, New York, on the night of Sunday, July 12, 1903, when a crowd beat Smith, a Black porter accused of assaulting a young girl in a boarding house. Citizens took him from the crowd to jail, and he was given a hearing before a judge.

Smith worked as a porter in Robert Jacobs's boarding house in Liberty, and the Washington Times described him as "formerly of New York." Mrs. E. H. Clarke and her two daughters occupied a room in the house.

According to a Liberty dispatch in the New-York Tribune, Smith broke into the Clarkes' room at about 9:30 p.m., and "it is charged" that he seized the younger child by the throat. Mrs. Clarke fought him and sent the children to rouse Harry L. May, a boarder in the next room. Smith's fingers were caught in a door as he followed Mrs. Clarke, and he fled into the street.

A crowd of about a thousand had gathered around the house, and Smith was "struck with clubs and roughly handled" while some shouted "Lynch him!" Citizens then took him from the mob and hurried him to jail. The officer in charge urged the crowd to "let the law take its course," and its leaders persuaded it to disperse.

Smith had a hearing before Judge Grant, which was adjourned to the following day, and he "persistently refused to say anything concerning himself." No report of the hearing's result, an indictment or a trial was found.

Two white dailies carried the story on July 14, 1903: the New-York Tribune under the headline "NEGRO ATTACKS A CHILD" and the Washington Times under "ANGRY MEN ATTEMPT TO LYNCH A NEGRO." The Tribune's subhead credited local citizens who "Barely Prevent a Lynching," while the Times dispatch from Middletown called the crowd "an infuriated mob" and treated "his attempted crime" as established. The Tribune gave the girls' ages as seven and eight, the Times as six and eight, and only the Tribune described the beating. No coverage in the Black press was found.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Eugene Smith
bases: A crowd struck the accused man with clubs amid cries of 'Lynch him!' before citizens removed him to jail; A2 headlined it an attempt to lynch (A1, A2).

A crowd of about a thousand acting without legal authority beat Smith over an accusation of assaulting a child and called for his lynching, but he was taken to jail alive, so no one was killed (A1, A2).
Two separately datelined reports, one telegraphed from Liberty and one from Middletown, agree that a mob nearly lynched Eugene Smith after the accusation (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Liberty telegraphed report
accounts.gist: Smith broke into Mrs. Clarke's room, seized the younger girl by the throat, fled when his fingers were caught in a door, and was clubbed by a crowd of about a thousand before citizens took him to jail.

accounts.label: Middletown dispatch
accounts.gist: Two girls aged six and eight were attacked by Smith, who narrowly escaped lynching by an 'infuriated mob' and then had a hearing before Judge Grant.

framing.detail: The Tribune headlined 'NEGRO ATTACKS A CHILD' and presented the charge as fact while describing the crowd's clubbing and the officer's appeal to let the law take its course.
The Washington Times headlined 'ANGRY MEN ATTEMPT TO LYNCH A NEGRO' and called the act 'his attempted crime' without qualification.

conflicts.note: The Liberty-datelined report (A1) is closer to the scene; neither is clearly better.
